title: The Strait of Hormuz in Global Economics
Strait of Hormuz Disruption, Africa–Asia Trade Linkages, and Policy Options for African States
items.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Disruption in and around the Strait of Hormuz can affect African economies even when African cargo does not directly transit the chokepoint. The relevant policy problem is therefore not limited to Gulf geopolitics or crude-oil pricing, but concerns the wider transmission of maritime insecurity into imported inflation, food systems, exchange-rate pressure, and state capacity. Objective: This article examines how a Hormuz disruption can transmit to African consumer prices through energy, freight, exchange-rate, fertilizer, and Asia-linked manufactures channels, while clarifying what available trade data can and cannot support. Methods: The study combines a structured integrative review with trade triangulation. Bilateral ITC Trade Map tables for Asia and the partner classification “Africa not elsewhere specified” for 2023–2025 are used only as residual micro-evidence because that category is not a defensible proxy for the African continent. Continent-scale inference is instead anchored in UNCTAD regional trade matrices and mechanism-specific evidence from the IEA, EIA, IMF, UNCTAD, World Bank, AfDB, FAO–WTO, IMO, and UKMTO. Results: The residual ITC series is exceptionally small, highly volatile, and heavily concentrated in machinery and electrical goods, confirming that Africa-wide vulnerability cannot be inferred from that bilateral category. The broader evidence shows that Africa’s exposure is principally indirect and systemic, operating through higher fuel and shipping costs, war-risk insurance, exchange-rate depreciation, fertilizer affordability, and the cost of Asia-sourced manufactures. Vulnerability is greatest where net fuel import dependence, shallow reserve buffers, non-pegged exchange-rate regimes, fertilizer dependence, and logistics fragility coincide. Conclusion: A Hormuz disruption should be understood by African policymakers not as an energy shock alone, but as a compound trade, inflation, and state-capacity shock. More credible responses therefore combine targeted social protection, transparent foreign-exchange prioritization, fertilizer-access strategies, corridor-efficiency reforms, and longer-run structural diversification.</jats:p>

title: THE HORMUZ STRAIT DISRUPTION AND PAYMENT DELAYS IN INDIAN TRADE FINANCE: A Time-Series Analysis of Banking Sector Vulnerability (2019-2024)
items.abstract: The Hormuz Strait—through which 21% of global petroleum trade passes—experienced significant geopolitical tensions from 2019-2024, creating disruptions to maritime commerce and financial flows. This paper provides a detailed empirical analysis of how these disruptions affected payment cycles in Indian trade finance and banking. Using Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data, port statistics, and transaction-level banking records (2019-2024, N=18,547 trade credit facilities), we employ time-series analysis, distributed lag models, and shock analysis to quantify the relationship between Hormuz disruptions and payment delays. Key findings: (1) Trade finance payment delays increased by an average of 8.3 days (95% CI: 6.1-10.5) following Hormuz tension announcements; (2) Letter of Credit (LC) issuance costs rose by 42-67 basis points; (3) Banks increased collateral requirements by 12-18%, contracting working capital availability by ₹4,200-6,800 crores; (4) The shock effect persisted for 90-120 days post-incident, with heterogeneous impacts across firm sizes (SMEs experienced 2.1x higher delays than large enterprises). Our analysis reveals that geopolitical shocks in maritime chokepoints generate significant financial friction in emerging market trade finance systems, with particular vulnerability among smaller firms lacking working capital buffers. We propose targeted policy interventions including development of trade credit insurance mechanisms, geographic diversification of banking relationships, and central bank communication frameworks for predictable intervention during crises.

title: GEOPOLITICAL SHOCKS AND GLOBAL MACROECONOMIC INSTABILITY: A SCENARIO-BASED STRUCTURAL VAR ANALYSIS OF THE 2026 ISRAEL-IRAN CONFLICT AND STRAIT OF HORMUZ DISRUPTION
items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper investigates the global macroeconomic transmission of the direct military escalation between Israel and Iran that culminated in the effective disruption of the Strait of Hormuz in February-March 2026. Using a Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) framework calibrated from the peer-reviewed literature of Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) and Kilian (2009), we construct three geopolitical scenariosswift resolution, prolonged blockade, and wider regional escalationand project the resulting impulse responses across global energy prices, equity markets, and inflation expectations. The pre-conflict Brent crude benchmark of $71.20/bbl and observed equity contractions of 4.5% (MSCI World) serve as empirical anchors for scenario calibration. Scenariosimulated Forecast Error Variance Decomposition (FEVD) projects that geopolitical risk innovations could account for up to 40% of energy price variance under a prolonged disruption, compared to a historical baseline of approximately 12%. The paper contributes a structured scenario framework for policymakers and central banks navigating the "war-inflation" regime that the 2026 conflict has initiated. All quantitative projections are scenario-based and clearly disclosed as such throughout.</jats:p>
